canonical_topic: Fast-start backup generation needed for wind ramp-down
definition: Because regional wind output can also drop off simultaneously across many turbines, the grid needs backup generation capable of starting and stopping very quickly to replace that lost output.
core_idea: When wind stops blowing across a region, many turbines can stop producing at once, forcing the grid to bring fast-start backup generation on- and off-line quickly; balancing is harder if that backup generation isn't located near the wind farms, since wind units themselves are typically sited in remote areas while fast-start units usually are not.
key_points: Wind output can fall off simultaneously across many turbines in a region when wind conditions change.
This requires backup (fast-start) generation to rapidly come on- and off-line to offset the loss.
Fast-start generators are typically not located in the same remote areas as wind farms, which complicates balancing power flows across the grid.
relationships: Transmission overload risk from correlated wind ramp-up
trading_implications: Wind's simultaneous ramp-down risk supports the case for flexible, quick-response capacity (e.g., fast-start gas peakers or battery storage) sited to help balance the grid when wind output drops.
